title: How Good Is The Cheapest Tour de France Bike? - X-LAB AD9

takeaways.text: The loaned size S, with Dura-Ace Di2, in-house cranks, 50 mm carbon-spoked wheels and 28 mm tyres, weighed 6.89 kg with a computer mount but no pedals.
They relay an XDS publicist's claim that its factories made over a quarter of the frames that won 2024 Tour de France stages; later both hosts say they reject the claim without evidence.
The in-house carbon-spoked wheels felt very stiff on rough roads; switching to alloy wheels with tubes transformed the ride for the presenter.
X-LAB told them it allows free swaps of the cockpit and cranks on top models such as the AD9 after a stock bike is ordered.
Living with it: a regular round steerer with standard spacers, a threaded bottom bracket and smooth-threading bolts; one seatpost part could fall into the frame.
At US$7,999 it undercuts other Tour de France bikes; the US$4,499 AD8 shares the frame mould with a heavier lay-up.

disclosure: X-LAB lent the size S bike, which went back afterwards; the presenter says X-LAB did not pay for or control the video. The description names Garmin as a channel sponsor.
summary: A July 2026 first look at a loaned size S X-LAB AD9 in team colours with Dura-Ace Di2, in-house cranks and carbon-spoked wheels, including a weigh-in and the company's component-swap policy. Its build differs from the mainland Vision-wheel build recorded here.
